domain_reasoning: The worker reads the case and writes the message, then sends it and logs it, but writing and reading take most of the time.
length_reasoning: A routine status reply from a template takes a few minutes; a claim-result or adjustment letter that must explain reasons and figures takes up to half an hour.
review_reasoning: A QA reviewer reads a short reply and checks it against the account; a typical one needs the facts checked against the case; a long claim letter needs figures and wording verified.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong answer or wrong claim outcome reaches the customer and causes a complaint or rework, but can be corrected.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's policies, claim rules, tone and account system, learned over a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: The analyst pulls and crunches result data, often with scripts or queries, but the final output is a report; the largest share is working with data tools and spreadsheets.
length_reasoning: A simple trend summary from a dashboard export takes a couple of hours; a multi-release analysis with flaky-test and defect trends takes a couple of days.
review_reasoning: A manager reads a short report and checks a few numbers; a typical one needs the data pulls and trend claims spot-checked; a large one needs the method and sources checked.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong trend or recommendation misdirects test effort or release decisions, but is usually caught later and reversible.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the product's test suites, data sources and history of flaky tests, built over several weeks to months.

domain_reasoning: The worker looks up the account or order in the system and compares it to what was promised, so most time is operating business systems.
length_reasoning: A simple check is a quick look at the account; one needing several systems or a discrepancy write-up takes longer.
review_reasoning: A supervisor opens the case and the account and confirms the change; a discrepancy case needs more tracing.
stakes_reasoning: A missed failed fix means the customer's problem persists and they call back, which is reversible.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's account and order systems and how changes appear in them, learned in a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: The work is writing the ticket in the tracker and attaching evidence, with reproduction steps as text; operating the tracker and capturing evidence take most of the time.
length_reasoning: A clear defect takes ten minutes to write up; an intermittent one needs re-reproduction, logs and narrowing, taking an hour.
review_reasoning: A developer or triage lead reads a clear ticket quickly; a typical one needs steps to be followed for reproduction; a hard one needs logs examined.
stakes_reasoning: A poor report wastes developer time or delays a fix, but is caught in triage and corrected.
context_reasoning: Needs the product, its components and team's triage conventions, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: Beyond talking, the time goes into looking up rates and operating billing or payment systems.
length_reasoning: A simple quote and payment takes a few minutes; setting up a payment plan or deposit with a complicated service takes longer.
review_reasoning: A reviewer listens to the contact and checks the charge and payment record against the rate rules; a long contact takes more checking.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong charge or mishandled payment causes financial loss or a billing dispute and money must be reconciled.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's rates, billing rules and payment systems, learned over several weeks.

domain_reasoning: The worker pulls records from several systems and outside information and reads them, mostly operating systems and looking things up.
length_reasoning: A simple bill complaint is checked in a quarter hour; a complex one involving usage history, weather and several records takes about two hours.
review_reasoning: A supervisor reads the finding and checks the key records; a typical one needs the evidence re-checked; a long one needs the chain of reasoning followed.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong validity finding leads to a wrong remedy or refund, or an unfair rejection, which may become a formal complaint.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's records, billing rules and typical causes of complaints, built over a few months.

domain_reasoning: The worker selects codes and writes a summary in the CRM, with the typing and field selection taking the time.
length_reasoning: A routine call is wrapped up in about a minute; a complex one with several actions takes several minutes.
review_reasoning: A QA reviewer reads a short record against the call; a typical one needs the codes checked; a long one needs the call itself consulted.
stakes_reasoning: A poor record causes confusion for later agents or inaccurate reporting, but is cheap to fix.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's disposition codes and notes conventions, picked up in a couple of weeks.

domain_reasoning: While the customer talks, the worker types notes into the account record, so the time is spent in the CRM.
length_reasoning: The whole contact is counted: a simple inquiry is a few minutes; a complaint with multiple actions runs to fifteen.
review_reasoning: A reviewer listens to the contact and reads the notes against it; longer contacts take longer.
stakes_reasoning: Missing or wrong notes cause rework or confusion for later agents, but can be corrected.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's systems and note conventions, learned in a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: Most time goes into imaging, installing software and creating accounts through admin consoles and tools, with some hands-on setup.
length_reasoning: A standard image with few accounts takes an hour of hands-on work; a specialist machine with unusual software and handover takes several.
review_reasoning: A supervisor checks the ticket and spot-checks the machine; a typical one needs a checklist walk-through; a specialist build needs more verification.
stakes_reasoning: A missed misconfiguration shows up when the employee starts and is fixed with a follow-up visit, though a security gap could matter.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's images, software catalogue, accounts and security standards, learned over a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: The worker pulls data from the tracker and builds counts and charts in tools, then writes a short summary; tool operation dominates.
length_reasoning: A routine weekly report from a dashboard takes under half an hour; a sprint report with blocker analysis takes a couple of hours.
review_reasoning: A manager reads the counts and checks a few numbers; a typical one needs the tracker queries checked; a long one needs the blockers verified.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong count misinforms the team but is noticed and corrected in the next report.
context_reasoning: Needs the project's tracker setup, workflow states and team conventions, learned in a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: The work is installing and configuring servers, software and network settings, much of it through scripts and configuration files.
length_reasoning: A small environment from existing templates takes a day; a large production mirror with data and tuning takes several days.
review_reasoning: A QA lead checks configuration against the specification and runs smoke tests; a larger environment takes much longer to compare.
stakes_reasoning: A mismatch makes performance results misleading, which can lead to wrong release decisions; this is found late.
context_reasoning: Needs deep knowledge of the production architecture, configurations and tooling, built over months.

domain_reasoning: The worker writes the procedure as a document following a template and standards, with text being the output.
length_reasoning: A short procedure takes under an hour; a complex one needing a rerun to confirm steps and screenshots takes a day.
review_reasoning: A QA lead reads a short document for completeness and standards; a typical one needs steps followed; a long one needs a trial execution.
stakes_reasoning: Errors cause failed or inconsistent test runs, or audit findings if standards are not met, but are fixable.
context_reasoning: Needs the product, test tooling and the employer's documentation standards, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The worker researches products, reads specs and writes up the evaluation, with a good share hands-on testing, but the output is a written document.
length_reasoning: A quick comparison of options takes a few hours; an evaluation with pilot testing and cost analysis takes several days.
review_reasoning: An IT manager reads a short evaluation and checks key claims; a typical one needs the criteria and costs checked; a long one needs the evidence assessed.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong recommendation can lead to a costly purchase or upgrade that is hard to reverse.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's environment, needs and purchasing norms, built over months.

domain_reasoning: The worker edits test code and runs it in the pipeline until it passes, which is code work.
length_reasoning: A small locator fix takes half an hour; a large product change that breaks many scripts takes a day or more.
review_reasoning: A code reviewer reads a small diff and sees the pipeline pass; a typical change needs the diff understood against the product change; a large one needs a deeper read.
stakes_reasoning: A faulty script gives false passes or flaky failures, found in later runs and fixed, though false passes can let bugs through.
context_reasoning: Needs the test framework, codebase and product, learned over weeks to months.

domain_reasoning: The worker reads the document and writes comments, with text as input and output.
length_reasoning: A short spec takes under an hour; a long design or compliance document takes a day.
review_reasoning: A lead needs to read the document and check that the findings are right and nothing is missed, which takes a good fraction of the original reading time.
stakes_reasoning: Missed errors in a document lead to later defects or compliance gaps, found downstream and reworked.
context_reasoning: Needs the product, domain and applicable standards, built over months for deep technical review.

unit_flag_reason: A single standard and a full set of release-readiness criteria are very different in scope, so the item mixes light and heavy work.
domain_reasoning: The work is writing and consulting stakeholders to produce a document.
length_reasoning: Updating a short checklist of criteria takes a few hours; developing a new standard with stakeholder input takes days of active work.
review_reasoning: A manager reads a short criteria list and judges it; a typical standard needs a careful read against practice; a full standard needs consideration with stakeholders.
stakes_reasoning: A weak standard lets poor-quality releases through or blocks good ones, with effects across many releases, but it can be revised.
context_reasoning: Needs deep knowledge of the organisation's product risks, release process and history, built over months.
